extracted.intended_audience: event organizers, aspiring cartoonists, and professionals seeking to learn/apply humor
extracted.subtask_description: Promotional speaker-page describing talks and workshops on creating cartoons, winning caption contests, fostering creativity, perseverance in submission, and applying humor in professional settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Yorker cartoon selection / increasing Caption Contest odds
rubrics_metrics.description: Bob Mankoff 'sees over a thousand cartoons a week in order to help select the fifteen or so that go into the magazine', and in his talks he explains the 'soup-to-nuts process of cartoon creation' and 'how to increase your odds of winning the famous New Yorker Caption contest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains editorial selection pressures (very high volume, extreme scarcity) and the kinds of cartoons that are chosen; includes discussion of cartoons that some readers 'don't get' and what that reveals about selection criteria. Presented as a fast-paced multimedia look at selection and captioning practice rather than a prescriptive checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose your ideas, imagination & wit to enhance creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: From 'The Naked Cartoonist' talk: pursue creativity by exposing your ideas, imagination, and wit to develop and enhance creative output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance includes finding your personal voice and message, learning from the masters of the past, transforming a current event into a 'comic tour-de-force', and even unconventional tips such as 'incorporate telling lies and taking naps into your daily routine.' Emphasizes that techniques apply to both aspiring cartoonists and anyone facing a blank page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor for personal and professional wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor has three main benefits: it blocks stress (physical and psychological health), makes us mentally flexible (manage change, take risks, think creatively), and serves as a social lubricant (improves effectiveness with colleagues and clients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk presents exercises and illustrative materials (pictures, cartoons, stories) to experience these benefits; intended as practical training for general audiences to integrate humor into daily life for improved effectiveness and resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and submission volume as a path to success
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in getting cartoons published requires perseverance: Mankoff cites his own path—three years and about 2,000 submissions before publication—arguing that persistence, not just talent, is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a motivational and practical program ('A Passion for Perseverance') teaching how to 'stop worrying and love the process of creating'; encourages readiness for the long haul while making the process enjoyable and interactive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for using humor in sales, marketing, and customer service
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor in advertising and customer interactions works in multiple ways: it creates rapport, overcomes sales resistance, opens customers' minds, increases message retention by involving customers, and can provide unexpected delight or repair customer relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk explores six ways humor works with customers, uses pictures/videos/cartoons/stories/exercises, and examines crucial differences between men's and women's humor and their implications for business messaging and customer relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourced humor lessons from caption contests
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker caption contest process: the magazine provides a captionless cartoon, readers submit captions, editors choose three finalists, and readers vote; millions of submissions from hundreds of thousands of participants produce empirical insight into what makes people laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff analyzes what crowdsourced captions reveal about humor and then runs audience-participation caption challenges (sponsor-provided cartoons), selecting finalists and staging live competitions; lessons focus on audience tastes and the dynamics of collective humor selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying humor to specific professions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailored talks under 'Laughter and the Professions' address how humor applies to domains such as law, healthcare, education, business executives, and mental health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each profession-specific session explores the role and benefits of humor in that field and includes applicable exercises, stories, and illustrative cartoons to demonstrate domain-relevant uses and boundaries of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and cultural history as a source of comedic insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Talks such as 'Funny You Should Ask: How & Why Jews Became "The People of the Joke"' use personal narrative and historical context to explain the development and character of a cultural humor tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses autobiographical detail and an illustrated cartoon history to show how upbringing and cultural venues (e.g., Borscht Belt) shaped comedic sensibilities; presented as both scholarly and personal perspective useful for understanding comedic content and perspective.
